name: Codeine and co-codamol
summary: Codeine is an opioid painkiller used for pain such as pain after an operation or injury, and co-codamol is codeine combined with paracetamol for aches and pains. The NHS lists constipation, drowsiness and sickness as common effects, and says it is possible to become addicted to codeine. Co-codamol contains paracetamol, so taking other paracetamol-containing medicines as well can lead to too much paracetamol, which can harm the liver.
class: Opioid analgesic (codeine, alone or combined with paracetamol)
usedFor: Codeine is used to treat pain, for example after an operation or injury.
Co-codamol is used for aches and pains such as period pain, muscle pain and toothache.
Co-codamol is often used when other painkillers, such as paracetamol on its own, have not worked.
howItWorks: Codeine is an opioid that acts on the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation. Co-codamol adds paracetamol, another painkiller, to the codeine.
onset: The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.

common: Constipation, feeling sick or being sick, and feeling sleepy or tired.
Sleepiness is reported to ease within a few days as the body gets used to codeine, but constipation tends to continue.
serious: An allergic reaction, slow or shallow breathing, an unusual heartbeat or low blood pressure are listed by the NHS as uncommon serious effects; breathing difficulty or a seizure needs a 999 call.

Repeated use can lead to dependence, abuse and addiction, which may result in life-threatening overdose, and the risk rises with higher doses and longer use; a prescriber or pharmacist can be asked about concerns.

Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms such as agitation, anxiety, palpitations, difficulty sleeping, shaking, sweating, body aches and restlessness, so the prescriber plans a gradual reduction.
Regular use can lead to tolerance, meaning higher amounts are needed to control pain over time.

cautions: Codeine is not suitable for everyone: the NHS lists allergy to codeine or other medicines, lung problems, a head injury, adrenal gland problems and kidney or liver problems among reasons it may not be suitable.
Codeine is not given to children under 12, and the NHS says it should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had tonsils or adenoids removed for sleep apnoea.
The NHS says codeine can be taken in pregnancy, but long-term use is not recommended, and use late in pregnancy can leave a newborn dependent so the baby may need extra observation in hospital.
The NHS says codeine and co-codamol are not taken while breastfeeding, because small amounts pass into breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby.
Alcohol can increase the risk of side effects and make a person very sleepy.
Recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin raise the risk of serious side effects with codeine.
The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery when feeling sleepy.
Co-codamol contains paracetamol, so other paracetamol-containing medicines, such as some cold and flu remedies, add to the total and the label of every product is checked.
monitoring: The NHS says the prescriber discusses how to lower the risk of addiction and how to reduce treatment gradually before stopping, and codeine is prescribed for the shortest time needed.

sections.heading: What are codeine and co-codamol used for?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid painkiller that the NHS describes as a medicine for pain, for example after an operation or injury.

Co-codamol is a combination of two painkillers, paracetamol and codeine. It is used for aches and pains, including period pain, muscle pain and toothache. It is often used when other painkillers, such as paracetamol on its own, have not worked.

The NHS says most adults can take codeine, but it is not suitable for everyone. Young people aged 12 to 18 are given it only if everyday painkillers have not worked, and it is not given to children under 12.

Product leaflets show that co-codamol comes in different strengths, and the NHS says side effects are more likely with the higher strengths.

sections.heading: How do codeine and co-codamol work?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid. The NHS says it acts on pain receptors in the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation.

In co-codamol the codeine is combined with paracetamol. The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.

sections.heading: Side effects, constipation and dependence
sections.body:
The most common side effects of both medicines are constipation, feeling or being sick, and feeling sleepy or tired. Sweating is also listed for codeine. The NHS says most of these, apart from constipation, tend to ease with time.

Because codeine slows digestion, constipation is one of the effects that may continue. The NHS suggests drinking more fluids and eating more fibre, and says a pharmacist or doctor can advise on a laxative if that does not help.

The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, and that regular use can lead to tolerance, meaning higher amounts are needed to control pain over time. Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms, so the prescriber plans a gradual reduction. Withdrawal can include agitation, anxiety, palpitations, difficulty sleeping, shaking, sweating, body aches and restlessness.

Serious allergic reactions are rare, and the NHS says to call 999 for breathing difficulty or a seizure.

sections.heading: Paracetamol in co-codamol and other medicines
sections.body:
Co-codamol contains paracetamol. The product leaflets say that anything else containing paracetamol should not be taken at the same time, and that cold and flu remedies are among the products worth checking.

The NHS says that taking too much co-codamol can be harmful and may need treatment, and the leaflets say too much paracetamol can cause delayed, serious liver damage.

Anyone who may have taken too much co-codamol, or too much paracetamol across several products, is advised to get medical help even if they feel well, through NHS 111 or, in an emergency, 999.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy, driving and alcohol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists an allergy to codeine or other medicines, a lung problem, a head injury, adrenal gland problems, and kidney or liver problems among the reasons codeine may not be suitable. It also says codeine should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had their tonsils or adenoids removed because of sleep apnoea. A pharmacist or doctor can say whether it suits a particular person, because the NHS notes it is not suitable for everyone.

The NHS says codeine and co-codamol can be taken in pregnancy, but long-term use is not recommended. Codeine used near the end of pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in a newborn, so the baby may need extra time in hospital for observation.

The NHS advises against taking codeine or co-codamol while breastfeeding, because small amounts reach breast milk and could cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. Plain paracetamol is the usual alternative.

The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery when feeling sleepy. Alcohol can add to sleepiness and raise the risk of serious side effects. Recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin also raise the risk of serious side effects.

faqs.q: Can you become addicted to codeine?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, and that regular use can lead to tolerance. The prescriber explains how the risk is reduced, and the dose is lowered gradually before stopping because stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal.
The NHS says codeine slows down digestion, which is why it can cause constipation. The NHS suggests more fluids and fibre, and a pharmacist or doctor can advise on a laxative if that does not help.

faqs.q: Can co-codamol be taken with other paracetamol medicines?
faqs.a: Co-codamol already contains paracetamol, and the product leaflets say not to take anything else containing paracetamol with it. Cold and flu remedies are among those worth checking, because too much paracetamol can cause liver damage.
The NHS advises against it, because small amounts of codeine pass into breast milk and could cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. A midwife, GP or pharmacist can explain alternatives.

faqs.q: Can you drink alcohol with co-codamol?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can make a person sleepier and increase the risk of serious side effects with co-codamol. The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery when feeling sleepy.
